articles.text: On a beautiful summer day, 219 seniors at Piedmont High School and Millennium High School graduated in a traditional ceremony at Witter Field. The event, held Friday June 11, was historic. It marked the first time in 15 months classmates and parents were together in one place after the COVID-19 pandemic caused the elimination of all public gatherings. The grandstands were full, the gowns were purple, and the sun shone brightly through a tapestry of high clouds in an undulating, rippling pattern. Seniors were seated in long rows on the field facing their families in the bleachers as the PHS band played Elgar’s “Pomp and Circumstance” to officially begin the ceremony. With a beaming smile, PHS Principal Adam Littlefield welcomed the graduates and their families on a day some thought might never happen. After more than a year of isolation, anxiety and change, everyone was there – teachers, students, family, and friends – collectively celebrating a most difficult year. Speakers emphasized the resilience of the students and the strength and adaptability of the parents. Salutatorian Anthony Wong said, “What has changed most are our perspectives. We think about life, ourselves, and others differently now. We’ve toughened up, we’ve found ourselves.” Co-Valedictorian Thomas Chu got everyone’s attention when he said, “All of my own greatest accomplishments in high school have been built upon failure. Life is not a steady vertical climb to the top, it is a vertical oscillating spring, where you have to go down to go up,” he said. His Co-Valedictorian Sam Eisenbach delivered a rousing speech that was partially a graduate seminar on physics, dealing with the relativity of time and the importance of community and shared experiences. “For the past fifteen months, our perception of time has been at the mercy of our isolation. But now, we have a unique opportunity to take time into our own hands. It’s about time that we un-pause our lives,” Eisenbach said. (To read his speech, see page 8.) articles.text: 26% of Piedmont residents own an electric vehicle Piedmont was recently given an award from the office of Gov. Gavin Newsom acknowledging the city’s efforts in accelerating the Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) market. The governor’s office created the award series, entitled ZEV Permitting Olympics, to honor counties that streamline permitting for electric vehicle charging stations that accelerate economic recovery. Alameda County received “gold” recognition, meaning that 100% of its jurisdictions have streamlined permitting for ZEV infrastructure. Alpine, San Francisco, Napa, and Tuolumne Counties also received gold status. In September 2020, Gov. Newsom signed an executive order to set a target that 100% of in-state sales of new passenger vehicles will be zero-emission by 2035. To help meet the challenge, the ZEV Permitting Olympics competition focuses solely on the creation and maintenance of electric vehicle charging stations. Piedmont supports residents in their effort to buy, lease, and drive electric vehicles. An online building permit application procedure allows residents to obtain a charger permit within three days. The City is also working with East Bay Community Energy in order to expand EV charging opportunities in public spaces around Piedmont. Currently, 26% of Piedmonters own an electric vehicle. More information on EV charger permits can be found on the city’s website at https://piedmont. ca.gov/services___departments/ planning _ _ _building/about_ building_/electric_vehicles.

When meaningful action trumps words By the Rev. Scott L. Denman St. Francis is known for that famous saying “preach the gospel, and if you have to, use words.” God is probably less concerned about what we believe and more concerned about the way we act. When we get right down to it, there are simply too many words flying around and not enough meaningful action. And as Christians approach Easter, the celebration of Jesus’ resurrection, it is easy for us to get sidetracked by words in the form of creeds, liturgies and theologies. These provide enough words to suffocate the real story that was all about meaningful action. It’s in that context that I share what I consider to be an Easter Story. A few years ago, Elizabeth Gilbert, author of “Eat, Pray, Love”, wrote about an incident that changed her life. She was riding the midtown bus in New York City in evening rush hour traffic. The weather was the worst January had to offer, complete with sleet and gusting wind. To quote her, “It sucked”. The bus was moving at a crawl, tempting her to get out and walk, but the cold icy world she was staring at through the window paralyzed her. The depression in that mobile metal tomb was palpable. Then something happened. When they arrived at 10th Street, the bus driver turned to address his gathered congregation in the bus. He said: “Ladies and Gentleman, we are now nearing the Hudson River. I’m going to ask you to do me a favor. When you get off the bus, I’m going to hold out my hand. As you walk past me, I want you to drop your troubles into the palm of my hand. I’ll take your troubles for you, and when I drive past the river, I’ll throw them in. The reason I want to do this is because you all seem like you’ve had a bad day, and I don’t want you taking all your worries and sorrows home to your friends and families now, because they deserve better than that, don’t they? So you just leave your troubles here with me to dispose of, and you all go have a wonderful night, OK?” Gilbert recounts: “The whole bus – the whole grumpy lot of us – broke into laughter. (Some of us, myself included, might have even shed a tear or two.) And one by one, as we filed off the bus, we dropped our troubles into the palm of this good man’s hand, and we stepped off the bus with smiles on our faces.” The resurrection stories of Christianity emerge in the context of darkness, struggle and despair, but proceed to inspire a radical shift of energy towards love, hope, justice, peace and kindness. Just as this man changed the energy in his mobile office, we too, might be inspired to embrace our power to positively change the energy in the contexts where we live. Maybe then we will know what it’s like to preach some good news, and – only if we have to – use words. The Rev. Scott Denman is Rector of St. John’s Episcopal Church, 1707 Gouldin Road in Montclair. articles.text: Residents invited to attend June 21 meeting City Council will consider the adoption of a housing item at its regularly scheduled meeting on Monday, June 21. Councilmembers will also consider an appeal of the state-mandated Regional Housing Needs Allocation, which requires that Piedmont produce over 500 new housing units within eight years. Residents are invited to attend and provide public comment during the meeting, which will be held via Zoom. Councilmembers will consider the adoption of Guiding Principles for implementing state-mandated Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU) programs, as well as objective design standards for the construction of apartment buildings. At the same meeting the city council will consider an appeal of the Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) that has been assigned to Piedmont. The mandated RHNA requires that Piedmont produce 587 new homes and apartments at fair pricing by the year 2031, the end of the next RHNA cycle. The expected allocation includes 163 very low income units, 94 low income units, 92 moderate income units, and 238 above-moderate income units. The role of local governments in the RHNA process is to participate in the development of the allocation methodology, and “to update their housing elements and local zoning to show how it will accommodate fair housing,” according to the Association of Bay Area Governments. A jurisdiction may file an appeal of its own draft RHNA allocation to request an increase or decrease in housing units. Palo Alto is set to appeal its regional housing allocation, and Clovis, which has been assigned 4,400 “high density housing” units, is also appealing. According to Pleasanton Weekly, that city is also considering an appeal, but is currently launching a “robust RHNA outreach process,” similar to Piedmont. For meeting agendas, staff reports, and more information, visit https://piedmont.ca.gov/government/city_council/meeting_ information___agendas.

articles.text: Editor: We have now seen no less than three different commentaries by Shirley Hooi, who has actively tried to persuade Piedmonters that not allowing PUSD to have classroom discussions in regards to current and historical race relations in America is preferential to addressing them. In her most recent letter to the editor she has cherry picked an Oregon School District policy that allegedly states, “being forced to find the correct answer for math is racist.” Ms. Hooi is aghast over this bastardized version of math and fears that our children will be rendered the laughingstock of the world because they are not forced to find the correct answer to a math problem. Partial credit is earned in almost any math class by showing all your work, assuming the process and order of operations to solve an equation is correct. For many teachers the “correct” answer isn’t a deal breaker. This standard practice of math instruction hasn’t rendered our kids unable to compete with their peers. articles.text: First-of-its-kind portal sets new standard for police transparency The Piedmont Police Department (PPD) has become the first law enforcement agency to launch a public Automatic License Plate Reader (ALPR) Transparency Portal, which will serve as a hub for the department’s ALPR usage, data retention, and access policies. The portal is a new offering from Flock Safety, the provider of the department’s ALPR camera system. “The opportunity to be the launching agency partner on this first-of-its-kind program underscores our deep commitment to openness, accountability, and integrity,” said Police Chief Jeremy Bowers. “The Piedmont Police Department strives to provide transparency on all police activities, policies, and practices, and Flock Safety’s Transparency Portal is another positive step in that direction,” Police Chief Jeremy Bowers said. “We recognize that the public has a right and responsibility to understand how the officers who are sworn to protect and serve them do their jobs.” The system provides Piedmont residents with anonymized audit logs of all police usage of ALPR technology. The portal displays usage statistics, to include the number of cameras the department owns and operates throughout the city and the other law enforcement agencies PPD shares data with. It also displays specific statistics on number of vehicles captured, as well as “Hot List” alerts - when neighborhood ALPR cameras capture a vehicle that is on the FBI’s National Crime Information Center (NCIC), a computerized index of criminal justice information available to Federal, state, and local law enforcement, the alert will be posted to the portal. “Flock Safety was founded four years ago based on the principle that it is possible to improve safety while protecting the critical right of citizen privacy,” Matt Feury, Flock Safety Co-Founder and CTO, said. “We place privacy, transparency, and bias mitigation at the forefront of our product development and are constantly engineering new features that encourage and align with our ethical principles. We’re excited for the Transparency Portal to serve as another tool that our law enforcement partners can use to strengthen ties with their communities.” To view the ALPR transparency portal, visit https:// transparency.flocksafety.com/ piedmont-ca-pd. articles.text: The time is 5:25 on June 11, 2021, 15 months after the World Health Organization first declared COVID-19 a pandemic. Has it really been that long? For many of us, it feels like our life has been on pause. For such a fundamental idea, the concept of time is inscrutable. What does it mean for time to pass? To truly understand time, we need a conceptual approach. We often think of time as an arrow, linear and rigid, projecting ever forward into the future. Physicists have formulated many arrows of time, but only the psychological arrow, the one we all experience collectively, is germane to our day-to-day lives. In a sense, we are all time travelers, proceeding forward at the constant rate of one second per second. However, our perception of time is anything but constant. When we look back on our experiences, certain periods of time feel as though they lasted longer than others. Think back to, say, the Homecoming Dance in freshman year. Remember the anticipation as you waited in line for a breathalyzer test [outside] Alan Harvey Theater, walking down to the quad to meet friends in the central tent, dipping Oreos in the chocolate fondue fountain, posing in sunglasses and frilly pink scarves in the photo booth, and dancing, ears ringing, as loud music blasted from the speakers in the student center. Despite it only happening over the course of a few hours, I have countless memories from the dance, and it feels like it lasted for days. Now think about a random day during quarantine, say November 16, 2020. Do you remember anything about that day? It barely feels like it even happened. Our perception of time is not static, but dynamic; not rigid, but malleable. It is not an individual experience, but a collective one. the pandemic made our lives less memorable, and as a result, it feels like the time passed in the blink of an eye. Community is essential for not only our memories, but for our sense of time itself. For the past 15 months, our perception of time has been at the mercy of our isolation. But now, we have a unique opportunity to take time into our own hands. It’s about time that we un-pause our lives. By connecting with others, we can appreciate our time and have more to remember. Let’s go out into the world and make our lives memorable. The speech of Valedictorian Sam Eisenbach was given at Piedmont High School’s graduation ceremony on June 11, 2021.

articles.text: Piedmont residents Pamela Schwartz and Dr. Steve Sidney are creating a summer program of talks by Kaiser Permanente community health leaders and preventive health researchers targeted primarily to high school students. articles.text: Piedmont Middle School’s graduation celebration, held on June 10, honored the 230 students in 8th grade. The ceremony featured four student speakers, a presentation from ASB members and congratulatory words from PMS administrators. The ceremony opened with 17 students welcoming the crowd in 17 different languages, a representation of the diverse background of the class. After welcoming remarks by Principal Ryan Fletcher, Dahlia Saffouri gave a speech as the first student speaker. “The past three years have been strenuous, and to some extent, a blur,” she said. “This has been the ultimate test, of not only our resilience, but also the strengths of our Wi-Fi networks, and the capacity of Schoology. As well as our own dilemmas, the country was in the middle of a polarizing election, California battled severe wildfires, and many of us partook in the Black Lives Matter marches to protest racial injustice. “With our newfound resilience and confidence, we are more than ready for the challenges ahead,” she said. Eighth grade speaker Inaya Majid said, “If this year has taught us anything, it is to look for the silver lining. As we slowly log off, whenever you come across a struggle, look back and remember this odd yet resilient year where we, students, teachers, families, all persevered. As we progress to high school and the future, we should go out into the world, face our unique challenges, and make no apologies for who we are.” The third student speaker, Faizan Kashmiri, described the journey to graduation as “a long, ever-twisting, roller-coaster ride. articles.text: Millennium High honored the 23 graduates of the 2021 class on Thursday, June 10 with a live ceremony at Witter Field. Normally, the ceremony is an intimate event at the Veterans Hall, but the event the last two years have been outdoors at Witter Field. The ceremony began with a welcoming address by Principal Shannon Fierro. Nick Safir, a MHS Paraeducator and high school baseball coach followed with remarks on the recent graduates. “I cannot thank this place and the class of 2021 enough for the amazing memories it has given me,” said Safir. MHS Student Body President Blaise Harrison gave a lively speech, thanking her peers and the Millennium staff. “We’ve had a wild run of high school, but this adventure could not have been completed without each and every staff member,” she said. She then listed off every staff member and called them, “Important, unforgettable and incredibly impactful.” Perpetual school awards, presented at graduation each year, were presented to Ken Yale Leadership Award Blaise Harrison Millennium Spirit Award Victoria Houston Personal Achievement Award Samson Bhatti Seth Marason-Banquer Community Contribution Award Harmonee Ross Alyssa Ultreras Also congratulated for their excellence were: Nakilah Johnson, who was named Piedmont High School’s Outstanding Female Athlete. articles.text: West Edge Opera will perform outside this summer with a series of performances at Bruns Amphitheater in Orinda from July 24 through August 8. West Edge Opera, originally the Berkeley Opera, was created in 1979 by Cal professor Richard Goodman. The company, under music director Jonathan Khuner and general director Mark Streshinsky, focuses primarily on lesser-known, contemporary, and avant-garde operas. West Edge Opera’s summer productions are titled West Edge Festival with three programs of music. The festival has been conducted in unconventional performance spaces, including the abandoned 16th street train station, the Pacific Pipe warehouse, and in 2019, in Oakland’s Bridge Yard under the Bay Bridge. Bruns Amphitheater became the festival’s home for its 2021 season through a partnership with California Shakespeare Theater (Cal Shakes). Cal Shakes announced that it will be sharing the Bruns Amphitheater in Orinda this summer with other arts organizations. Berkeley Symphony, West Edge Opera, Destiny Arts and Bandloop are among the organizations who will perform or host events there. “What gives us our proverbial edge is that our venue at the Bruns is in the open air, which makes a big difference. articles.text: San Francisco’s American Conservatory Theater will present a special online screening of Armistead Maupin’s Tales of the City: The Musical, to stream on Broadway on Demand’s National Theater Network during San Francisco’s Pride Week, June 25-27. “As San Francisco returns and we celebrate Pride anew this month, I’m thrilled to have ACT’s beloved musical and Armistead Maupin’s characters be part of the celebration,” Director Pam MacKinnon said. “This is a show that deserved a longer life. We’re grateful to have this simple but beautiful archival capture that represents the city, where we were, and who we can be.” A week prior to the musical release affords you enough time to introduce, or re-introduce, yourself to Maupin’s series of novels chronicling the lives of fictional San Franciscans in the late 1970’s. Portions of the novels, which were adapted as a miniseries with Olympia Dukakis and Laura Linney, and again as a Netflix series in 2019 starring Elliot Page, were published as a newspaper serial in 1974 in Marin County’s The Pacific Sun, the longest running alternative weekly in the nation. The success of Maupin’s serial prompted the San Francisco Chronicle to pick it up two years later, and HarperCollins published it as a book two years after that in 1978. Tales of the City is a series of nine novels. They are binge-worthy and excellent beach, park, or overall-summer reads. The series begins with protagonist Mary Anne Singleton, a “naive young woman from Cleveland” who is visiting San Francisco for vacaLaura Linney (left) and Olympia Dukakis as Mary Anne Singleton and Anna Madrigal in the first television adaption of Armistead Maupin’s Tales of the City. tion and impulsively decides to stay after falling in love with the culture and “scene.” “The worst of times in San Francisco was still better than the best of times anywhere else,” was Mary Ann’s rationale to her mother for not returning to Ohio. San Francisco in the 1970’s becomes a character in itself in the series of novels and Maupin does a stellar job narrating and observing through the wide eyes of a Midwestern transplant. He was born in Washington D.C. and attended college at University of North Carolina in Chapel Hill but has always said that San Francisco is where he feels most at home. Tales of the City covers a group of misfits, 20-and-30- somethings in one house located at the fictional 28 Barbary Lane, headed by Anna Madrigal. Maupin is widely accepted in the literary community as one of the first writers to address the subject of the AIDS epidemic in his 1983 novel Babycakes, a continuation of the “Tales” series. Of the autobiographical nature of his characters, he said, “I’ve always been all of the characters in one way or another.” The book series in the 70’s and 80’s served as a sparkling, semi-soap opera. Reviewers on GoodReads.com affectionately call it a “time capsule” and “an indelible portrait of an era that changed forever the way we live.” The series evolved into a Netflix drama and addressed, 40 years later, gentrification and how the “dot-com boom” rattled native San Franciscans. Maupin’s laughout-loud narration is all, clearly, an homage to the city he loves - he wrote in his first in the series, “if [Mary Anne Singleton] ever had a child, she would want him to grow up in San Francisco - where Mardi Gras was celebrated five times a year.” Netflix’s Tales of the City was released one year before Olympia Dukakis passed away. For information on how to watch ACT’s musical adaption, visit www.act-sf.org/whatson/20202122-season/tales-of-thecity.

articles.text: Let the royal family of England enjoy the crown jewels. Simple pleasures are often the best. This philosophy was driven home to me on Saturday afternoon, and it came as an unexpected surprise. My wife suggested an early dinner at Anaviv in Richmond. Surprisingly, it isn’t in downtown Richmond. Quite the opposite. It is situated just off Highway 580 near the entrance to the San Rafael bridge and appears to be more a parking lot than a restaurant. But don’t let that bother you. The restaurant itself has a Spartan ambience. Everything is outdoors. There is a woodfired oven, simple tables and chairs, and a few umbrellas. What Anaviv lacks in ambience, they compensate with enthusiasm. Service is good and so is the food. The menu is modest. There are a few starters and snacks. We chose charcoal roasted asparagus ($12). The slender spears of asparagus were charcoal roasted to perfection and served with an elegant sauce. For our main dish, we chose a pizza margarita ($20) and added some hen of the woods mushrooms. You could imagine that you were in a simple outdoor restaurant in Naples, enjoying a soft crust pizza while the hot sun beats down. (Remember to wear a hat on sunny days.) For dessert we ordered a beautiful combination of ube and avocado ice cream with a jellied coconut panna cotta. Curiously, the waitress brought the panna cotta at the same time as the pizza. Upon request, they brought it back at the end of the meal. Anaviv has live musical entertainment three days a week. The food in the restaurant is well worth the price. But when you add in the entertainment, it is an amazing bargain. The show began with a few flamenco guitar solos. It was apparent from the beginning that the show would be memorable. The guitarist’s stage name is Keni el Lebrijano. Close your eyes when you listen and you’ll be transported to a gypsy cave in Seville or Granada. It was obvious to me from the first notes that Keni lives and breathes flamenco. In a few minutes he was joined by two women and a man. The entire audience became energized with excitement. The man began to sing in authentic canto hondo style. He looked the part and sang with the passion that is so characteristic of a great flamenco singers. The two women took turns on the dance floor. You could tell that the audience was really appreciating the music. A woman from the audience got up and started to dance. She was every bit a professional dancer, but her performance was impromptu. I spoke with her during the break, and she told me that she is a professional dancer. It turns out that she was the dance partner of one of my school classmates. She is Andrea la Canela. They say that people are beginning to travel internationally once again. Travel is still a hassle. Do yourself a favor. You don’t need to go to the Gypsy caves in Seville. Anaviv will do just fine.
articles.title: Flamenco and pizza in Richmond

articles.text: 2021-22 season opens with Mozart and Salieri Opera San Jose has announced its 2021-22 season, to include in-person performances beginning this November in the California Theatre. The season launches with a production of Rimsky-Korsakov’s Mozart and Salieri, followed by Purcell’s Dido and Aeneas, Bizet’s Carmen, and Bernstein’s West Side Story to close. “This season, we explore the necessity of human connection. We explore love—and love interrupted. We witness people who are confronted by a world incompatible with who they are or who they wish to be,” General Director Khori Dastoor said. Mozart and Salieri, a Heiman Digital Media Studio production, will begin as a live-streamed capture in September. Subscribers will receive access to the production. Based on Alexander Pushkin’s play of the same name, the psychological drama follows the Italian composer Antonio Salieri and his envy of Mozart’s musical genius. Conducted by Donato Cabrera and directed by Fenlon Lamb, the play incorporates quotations from Mozart’s Requiem and Don Giovanni; Baritone Sidney Outlaw stars as Salieri. Dido and Aeneas will launch Opera San Jose’s return to live performances, beginning on November 13. Starting in November, patrons will enjoy earlier performance times. Evening performances will begin at 7:30 p.m., and matinees will begin at 2 p.m. For more information on COVID protocols and to obtain tickets to upcoming live performances, visit https:// www.operasj.org/subscriptions/. Patrons of Opera San Jose will return for live performances in California Theatre in November.
articles.title: Opera San Jose returns live in November

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony, under the guidance of consulting firm Elevated Diversity, will host a series of listening sessions that will provide “a crucial foundation for [the] work ahead,” said symphony Executive Director Jim Tibbs. It is one aspect of the symphony’s Inclusion, Equity, Diversity, and Access (IDEA) project, to begin this summer. “The sessions are intended to provide an opportunity for you to share your perspectives and insights relating to inclusion, diversity, equity, and access at Berkeley Symphony,” Tibbs said. The symphony was awarded a $19,500 grant from the League of American Orchestras, with the purpose of strengthening their understanding of diversity, equity and inclusion. Berkeley Symphony has engaged Elevated Diversity, a diversity, equity and inclusion consultancy and training organization based in California, to assist in engagement projects this summer. The organization’s mission is to help other organizations “create workplaces where diversity is viewed as a competitive strength and where inclusion is woven into the very fabric of our culture.” “We are beyond thrilled to have been selected to work with the Berkeley Symphony on this incredibly important initiative,” Founder of Elevated Diversity Rhonda Moret said. “Being arts lovers ourselves, we find the project to be highly engaging and without experience and expertise working with other organizations in the arts space, we feel like we are the perfect group to ensure the effort a successful one.” A listening session is similar to a “focus group” in which participants are asked to candidly share their experiences and answers on-topic questions. The goal of these sessions is to better understand the opportunities, and challenges, surrounding a topic as each individual perceives them. Sessions will be conducted via Zoom, and are designed as a set-structured roundtable discussion. Those who wish to participate in a listening session may register your interest via a Google form at https://docs.google.com/ forms/d/e/1FAIpQLScg9-6l5r7BpqWcNXyHIXmmRtoMFxA6wgm-HBZUpawriOv8lw/viewform. Berkeley staff will reach out to interested participants about next steps. These sessions will last approximately one hour.
articles.title: Berkeley Symphony hosts listening sessions in diversity project

articles.text: The First Mondays Reading Group, sponsored by the Recreation Department, welcomed Piedmont author Shanti Brien at its June 7 meeting for a discussion about her recently released book Almost Innocent. Fifteen readers called in to talk with her. Participating were: Mike Bandrowski, Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Margie Blodgett, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Albert Chen, Pat McSwain, Alicia Rivera, Sally Arney, Jamie Forsythe, Dick Carter, and discussion leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. Brien is a criminal defense attorney and the wife of a former NFL player. In Almost Innocent, she writes about our criminal justice system based upon her own experience and the stories of nine of her previously convicted felon clients. The conversation took place before the group’s regular June discussion of President Obama’s new memoir, A Promised Land. Brien did a brief reading from her book, made some comments, and then opened the talk to accept questions. She said that her clients were happy to be included in the book so that their stories would be told. Her hope is that these and other, similar situations will create “radical empathy” for injustice in the system; and that some reform will result. Shanti said that everyone can do something. One of the most basic things is for voters to make informed choices about district attorneys, who have great control in the system. She also talked about the process of writing a book. It took nearly three years to initially write the book, and another two to three years of editing, plus five years to find an agent. Publishers are hesitant about first time authors because the financial uncertainty associated with them. The profit margins associated with publishing are thin. Publishers prefer proven authors or established “personalities.” She encouraged anyone with a desire to write a book to “just start writing chunks” of content. The 40-minute conversation was highly enjoyable and informative. For more information, visit: https://www.shantibrien.com/. A Promised Land This memoir by former President Barack Obama (2009-2017) was published in November 2020 and is the first of a planned two-volume series. The book covers Obama’s life from his early years through the events surrounding the killing of Osama bin Laden in May 2011. The book has received good reviews from the New York Times, The Washington Post, and The Guardian. Commercially, it has been extremely successful and was on the New York Times best-seller list in non-fiction for eight weeks. It is 768 pages long, has been translated into two dozen languages, and is also available as a 28-hour audiobook with Obama reading it in its entirety. The book is a unique, thoughtful, intimate, and revealing exploration of Obama’s personal and family lives. There are insights into the people and leaders with whom he interacted, as well as the impact pf presidential power. The readers agreed that Obama is a masterful writer and his prose is enjoyable to read. It was noted that he writes the way he talks, eloquently and expansively. The group especially enjoyed the details about Obama’s life and personal anecdotes. He describes his relationship and interactions with his wife, Michelle, shows her strength and importance during his presidency. The candid impressions of world leaders are fascinating, including the events leading up to the killing of Osama bin Laden. While the positive aspects of the book are undeniable, some readers had issues. Obama’s writing covers all facets of an issue, action, or event. All the details can be a challenge, especially with situations that are most appealing to politicians and public policy makers. The book’s length can also be a challenge, and some readers found it tedious at times. Some found it more of a history book than a memoir. The group said it was pleased to have selected and read A Promised Land. Additionally, the book reminded many of what it was like just a short time ago in our nation, and candidly in a happier time. With their book conversations complete, the group discussed future books to read. For July they had previously selected the timely fiction Interior Chinatown by Charles Yu. For August, September, and October respectively, they picked The Fire Next Time by James Baldwin, Deacon King Kong by James McBride, and Nomadland by Jessica Bruder. The group will meet next in a Zoom call on Monday, July 5, at 1:30 p.m. New members are always welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required by contacting John Wilk at jwilk@piedmont.ca.gov.

pages.text: Wednesday, June 16, 2021 23 FIRST MONDAYS READING GROUP First Monday book group discusses Brien book By Dick Carter The First Mondays Reading Group, sponsored by the Recreation Department, welcomed Piedmont author Shanti Brien at its June 7 meeting for a discussion about her recently released book Almost Innocent. Fifteen readers called in to talk with her. Participating were: Mike Bandrowski, Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Margie Blodgett, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Albert Chen, Pat McSwain, Alicia Rivera, Sally Arney, Jamie Forsythe, Dick Carter, and discussion leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. Brien is a criminal defense attorney and the wife of a former NFL player. In Almost Innocent, she writes about our criminal justice system based upon her own experience and the stories of nine of her previously convicted felon clients. The conversation took place before the group’s regular June discussion of President Obama’s new memoir, A Promised Land. Brien did a brief reading from her book, made some comments, and then opened the talk to accept questions. She said that her clients were happy to be included in the book so that their stories would be told. Her hope is that these and other, similar situations will create “radical empathy” for injustice in the system; and that some reform will result. Shanti said that everyone can do something. One of the most basic things is for voters to make informed choices about district attorneys, who have great control in the system. She also talked about the process of writing a book. It took nearly three years to initially write the book, and another two to three years of editing, plus five years to find an agent. Publishers are hesitant about first time authors because the financial uncertainty associated with them. The profit margins associated with publishing are thin. Publishers prefer proven authors or established “personalities.” She encouraged anyone with a desire to write a book to “just start writing chunks” of content. The 40-minute conversation was highly enjoyable and informative. For more information, visit: https://www.shantibrien.com/. A Promised Land This memoir by former President Barack Obama (2009-2017) was published in November 2020 and is the first of a planned two-volume series. The book covers Obama’s life from his early years through the events surrounding the killing of Osama bin Laden in May 2011. The book has received good reviews from the New York Times, The Washington Post, and The Guardian. Commercially, it has been extremely successful and was on the New York Times best-seller list in non-fiction for eight weeks. It is 768 pages long, has been translated into two dozen languages, and is also available as a 28-hour audiobook with Obama reading it in its entirety. The book is a unique, thoughtful, intimate, and revealing exploration of Obama’s personal and family lives. There are insights into the people and leaders with whom he interacted, as well as the impact pf presidential power. The readers agreed that Obama is a masterful writer and his prose is enjoyable to read. It was noted that he writes the way he talks, eloquently and expansively. The group especially enjoyed the details about Obama’s life and personal anecdotes. He describes his relationship and interactions with his wife, Michelle, shows her strength and importance during his presidency. The candid impressions of world leaders are fascinating, including the events leading up to the killing of Osama bin Laden. While the positive aspects of the book are undeniable, some readers had issues. Obama’s writing covers all facets of an issue, action, or event. All the details can be a challenge, especially with situations that are most appealing to politicians and public policy makers. The book’s length can also be a challenge, and some readers found it tedious at times. Some found it more of a history book than a memoir. The group said it was pleased to have selected and read A Promised Land. Additionally, the book reminded many of what it was like just a short time ago in our nation, and candidly in a happier time. With their book conversations complete, the group discussed future books to read. For July they had previously selected the timely fiction Interior Chinatown by Charles Yu. For August, September, and October respectively, they picked The Fire Next Time by James Baldwin, Deacon King Kong by James McBride, and Nomadland by Jessica Bruder. The group will meet next in a Zoom call on Monday, July 5, at 1:30 p.m. New members are always welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required by contacting John Wilk at jwilk@piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: The Number 11 streetcar on the right-of-way between Linda and Sunnyside Avenues in 1948. was what then was the newly built Transbay Terminal in San Francisco. Cars travelled east and west on the top level of the bridge. Electric trains served other parts of the East Bay. The A Train covered downtown Oakland, and the B Train travelled through the Lakeshore and Trestle Glen neighborhoods. The E Train went to Berkeley to the Claremont Hotel. In Berkeley, the F Train travelled on Shattuck to Solano, the G Train served Westbrae, the H Train travelled on Monterey Avenue, and the K Train ran on College Avenue. Today, some AC Transit buses use the same letters to identify their routes. End of the Line The last Piedmont streetcar operated until 1948. With the proliferation of automobiles after World War II, electric streetcars were no longer considered efficient. Buses, later run by AC Transit District, took over the streetcar routes. The C Train continued to run to San Francisco until 1958 when streetcars on the Bay Bridge were discontinued. The Oakland Tribune described this poignant time as “sad, exuberant, quiet, noisy, confused and orderly.” That last ride was standing room only. Homeowners along the train’s route came out to wave goodbye, as the motorman saluted back. The C Train at the small Oakland Avenue station at Latham that provided shelter to waiting passengers in 1940. Legacy The Number 11 and 12 streetcar lines and the C Train also left a legacy of vacant right-ofway land. The right-of-way for the Number 11 between Sunnyside and Linda became the beautifully landscaped Linda Park and the energetic Linda Avenue Dog Park across from Beach School. The Number 12 streetcar on Fairview Avenue had no dedicated right-of-way. When the C Train stopped running, its right-of-ways were filled with houses. Today, three narrow houses occupy the right-of-way along Latham. The land between Ricardo and York became more back yard space for adjacent houses. New houses were built on York near Arroyo. The C Train also shared the right-of-way on Arroyo with the Number 10 streetcar before it As the C Train curves to the right toward its route to Latham and Oakland, the Number 10 streetcar descends Arroyo toward Piedmont Avenue.

articles.text: Wednesday Walkers pause for a group photo on Palm Drive on June 9. Pictured are: Albert Chen (left), Jim Kuo, Harriette Louie, Cheryl Coleman Jones, Alicia Rivera, Haybert Houston, Adrienne Hamlin, Melba Yee, Nancy Henn, Andree Greenberg, Brenda Ferrero, Nancy Olsen, Mark Greenberg, Sherry Jacobs, Larry Olsen, Cat Gustafson, and Bob Gustafson. With nearly perfect weather, the Walking on Wednesdays group had its biggest turnout so far this year with 18 people. The group was especially pleased to welcome first time walker Haybert Houston. The walkers enjoy local history and find it is often helpful to put what they see into a historical context. So, drawing once again on information provided by Gail Lombardi of the Piedmont Historical Society, an account of Piedmont’s early development was told. Gold was discovered in California at Sutter’s Mill in 1848 and the 49ers soon followed, many coming to San Francisco. Trees in the East Bay were cut to satisfy the construction needs. This opened large areas in the Oakland foothills, and what is now Piedmont, for ranches with livestock and grain. The Reed Ranch covered much of what is now Piedmont. In the 1860s a person bought part of the ranch and “rediscovered” a mineral spring that a Mr. Holmes had discovered years before. After Holmes died the springs were forgotten. However, as they were only three miles from the Oakland railroad station, the new owner thought a mineral spring with perceived health benefits was a big business opportunity. He recruited San Francisco investors and they built the Piedmont Springs Hotel in 1876 on the very spot where the Exedra stands today. The hotel burned down in 1892, but this created a new business opportunity. Frank C. Havens, a developer, bought the land and opened Piedmont Park in 1898 with the mineral springs and two grottos as attractions. Another attraction was a large hedge maze where Witter Field is today. The main entrance to the park was at the current bus stop across from the Wells Fargo bank, but visitors could also access the park by a path from Grand Avenue on what is now Palm Drive. The walkers decided to walk through Piedmont Park, see the site of the mineral springs with Havens’ grottos, and on to Palm Drive. They saw children playing near the upper grotto, and one exploring the drought-depleted water flow of Bushy Dell Creek. They took the lower path through the park to the site of the lower grotto, where they read a historical maker about Mark Twain’s visit to this location in 1868 when he was on a lecture tour in Oakland. On the marker there is a picture of the event with Twain identified. The group continued to another marker that showed the “Eucalyptus Amphitheater” that Havens built in 1908. The marker has a picture with a large group of the Sons of Norway holding annual meeting in 1915. They noted the location of Piedmont Play School for preschoolers. The school was moved to Hampton Field when Witter field and track were expanded in 1998. The walkers emerged from the park and read about Havens’ “Maze” on another historical marker. They entered Park View Avenue at the base of Witter Field, and followed Palm Drive, noting some unique, colorful homes and gardens. The majestic palm trees are over 125 years old, and are the last remaining trees that lined the path from Grand Avenue to the lower entrance of Piedmont Park and the Maze. The palms are in the front yards of the homes, not on city property. Sherry Jacobs, who lives nearby, told the group that some trees have been removed over the last few years. It had been a beautiful morning with lots of Piedmont history and good conversations with friends. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues). The gathering time is 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge, and new walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required by contacting jwilk@piedmont.ca.gov. In addition to aesthetic considerations, material selection always is a balancing act between quality and cost. More durable, longer-lasting materials generally cost more initially. Factoring in the true building-life costs, however, mitigates the differences. If, for example more expensive copper flashing and gutters are used, they are probably going to last the life of the building, whereas less expensive gutters of less durable materials will have to be replaced after a certain number of years. As any home remodeler knows, the decision-making required around material selection can be overwhelming. The process often has just begun with the actual selection of a material or product. The next decision may be size, then the choice of an available texture (the tactile surface) and then the colors. Most of the time selections are made from manufacturers’ standards, but often for a premium they can be custom made to the architects’ unique specifications. And finally, in the case of materials like masonry or brick, the laying pattern and coursing has to be decided.
